docs.title: Portcullis
docs.text:
Static security analyzer for CI/CD pipeline definitions — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins.

CI/CD pipelines hold repository secrets, carry write-capable tokens, and routinely execute code from untrusted pull requests. One misconfiguration turns that combination into full repository compromise. Portcullis detects those misconfigurations statically and — unlike a linter — ranks each finding by whether an attacker can actually reach the job it's in.

docs.title: Why Portcullis
docs.text:
• Three platforms, one model. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins are normalized into one shared model, so every rule runs on every platform.
  • Context is the ranking backbone. A finding inside a job reachable from an untrusted trigger is escalated one severity level — the merge-blocking P0 bucket is reserved for attacker-reachable criticals.
  • Static, offline, deterministic. Never executes your pipeline, never touches the network at scan time, and produces byte-identical output for the same input.
  • Four outputs. Canonical JSON, self-contained HTML (CSP-hardened), SARIF 2.1.0 (schema-validated), and PR-comment Markdown.
  • Honest. Every finding carries a confidence level; low-confidence findings never block a merge.

docs.title: 30-second start
docs.text:
pip install -e .          # from a checkout
portcullis scan . --fail-on P0

See Installation, the CLI Reference, and runnable Examples.

docs.title: The detection rules
docs.text:
Rule Catches R1 Dangerous triggers — pwn-requests, artifact poisoning, self-hosted runners on PRs R2 Expression injection — untrusted text into shell/script lines R3 Pinning — actions/images on mutable tags instead of SHAs/digests R4 Token permissions — over-broad / write-all / secrets: inherit R5 Secret exposure — echoed, argv-passed, untrusted-reachable, or hardcoded R6 Step integrity — curl \| bash, unverified downloads, insecure commands

Full catalog with false-positive notes: Detection Rules.

docs.title: Proven on real pipelines
docs.text: Run against 66 real pipeline files from 10 well-known OSS projects — zero crashes, sensible ranking, validated head-to-head against zizmor. See Real-world Evaluation and Benchmarks.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: Portcullis is usable as a library, not just a CLI. The package ships type hints (py.typed), so your editor and mypy see the full API.

docs.title: Scan a path
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from portcullis.core.engine import scan
from portcullis.core.models import ScanConfig

config = ScanConfig(
    platforms=frozenset({"github", "gitlab", "jenkins"}),
    trusted_action_prefixes=("myorg/",),   # optional
)
report = scan(Path("."), config)

print(report.score, report.priority_counts)
for f in report.findings:
    sev = (f.severity or f.base_severity).name
    print(f.rule_id, f.kind, f"{f.file_path}:{f.line}", sev, f.confidence.name)

docs.title: Render any format
docs.text:
Every emitter is a pure function of the Report:

from portcullis.emitters import emit_json, emit_html, emit_sarif, emit_markdown

json_text  = emit_json(report)      # canonical, deterministic
html_text  = emit_html(report)      # self-contained, CSP-hardened
sarif_text = emit_sarif(report)     # SARIF 2.1.0 (schema-validated)
md_text    = emit_markdown(report)  # PR-comment sized

docs.title: Key types
docs.text:
• portcullis.core.models.Report — the scan result (findings, score, priority_counts, files_scanned, skipped, suppressed).
  • portcullis.core.models.Finding — one traceable finding (rule_id, kind, file_path, line, base_severity, severity, escalated, confidence, priority, message, remediation, evidence).
  • portcullis.core.models.ScanConfig — scan options.
  • Enums: Severity, Confidence, Priority (all IntEnum; note Priority.P0 == 0 is falsy — always compare priority is not None).

A complete, runnable script is at examples/python_api.py.

docs.title: Determinism & safety
docs.text: The API inherits the tool's guarantees: it never executes pipeline content, performs no network access, and returns deterministic results (the now parameter to scan() lets you pin the timestamp for reproducible output in tests).

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
portcullis scan <path>
    --format {json,html,sarif,md,all}   default: html
    --out DIR                           default: ./portcullis-report
    --fail-on {P0,P1,P2,P3}             exit 1 if any finding is at/above this priority
    --platforms LIST                    subset of github,gitlab,jenkins
    --trusted-actions PREFIX            repeatable; treat prefix as first-party (lower R3 urgency)
    --quiet                             suppress the console summary
    -v, --verbose                       increase log verbosity (-v info, -vv debug; logs to stderr)
portcullis rules list                   print the rule catalog + false-positive notes
portcullis version

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 scan completed; nothing at/above the --fail-on threshold 1 findings at/above the --fail-on threshold (the gate tripped) 2 usage error (bad path, unknown platform)

The exit code is the integration point: portcullis scan . --fail-on P0 returns 1 to fail a CI step and block a merge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Scan the current repo, write an HTML report
portcullis scan .

# All four formats, gate on P0
portcullis scan . --format all --out ./report --fail-on P0

# Only GitHub Actions, treat your org's actions as first-party
portcullis scan . --platforms github --trusted-actions myorg/

# Verbose logging to stderr (does not pollute stdout / report output)
portcullis scan . -vv

# Print the rule catalog
portcullis rules list

docs.title: Suppressing a reviewed finding
docs.text:
Inline comments dismiss a finding without editing the tool — and are reported in every output so they're never silent:

- uses: example-org/tool@v3   # portcullis: ignore[R3]   (or bare: # portcullis: ignore)

// works for Jenkinsfiles. Place the comment on the finding's line or the line above it.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Portcullis logs to stderr (stdout is reserved for report/machine output) and is silent by default. -v raises to INFO, -vv to DEBUG. As a library, importing Portcullis never configures logging for the host application.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Runnable examples live in the examples/ folder.

docs.title: Scan a vulnerable repo
docs.text:
portcullis scan examples/vulnerable-repo --format all --out ./demo-report

examples/vulnerable-repo contains an inert-but-vulnerable workflow (a pwn-request plus expression injection). Expect a low score and P0 findings. Open demo-report/report.html.

docs.title: Scan a secure repo
docs.text:
portcullis scan examples/clean-repo

The same task done right — SHA-pinned, least-privilege, untrusted input routed through env:. Scores 100/100.

docs.title: Programmatic use
docs.text:
python examples/python_api.py examples/vulnerable-repo

See the Python API page.

docs.title: Add Portcullis as a CI gate
docs.text:
examples/portcullis-gate.yml is a copy-paste GitHub Actions job that fails the build on any P0 finding:

- name: scan pipelines (fail on P0)
  run: |
    pip install portcullis-scanner
    portcullis scan . --format sarif --out ./portcullis-report --fail-on P0

docs.title: The inert-example rule
docs.text: Every vulnerable example is vulnerable-looking, harmless-acting: echo payloads, example.com URLs, obviously-fake secret strings. They demonstrate the vulnerability classes without shipping working attacks.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Portcullis requires Python 3.11+ and has a single runtime dependency (ruamel.yaml).

docs.title: From a checkout
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/mk12002/Portcullis
cd Portcullis
pip install -e .            # editable install, exposes the `portcullis` command
portcullis version

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text:
Once published:

pip install portcullis-scanner

docs.title: Development install
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"    # adds pytest, ruff, mypy, jsonschema
pip install -e ".[docs]"   # adds mkdocs + mkdocs-material for the docs site

Run the checks:

pytest                     # 175 tests
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
mypy src/portcullis

docs.title: Verify it works
docs.text:
portcullis scan examples/vulnerable-repo --format all --out ./demo-report
# → a low score with P0 findings; open demo-report/report.html
portcullis scan examples/clean-repo
# → 100/100

docs.title: Requirements files
docs.text: requirements.txt (runtime) and requirements-dev.txt (dev + docs) mirror the pyproject.toml dependency groups for tooling that expects them. pyproject.toml is the canonical source of truth.

docs.title: Detection Rules
docs.text: Portcullis ships six rule families (R1–R6) plus a synthetic R0 for unparseable files. Run portcullis rules list for the live catalog with false-positive notes. Each rule operates on the normalized model, so it applies to every platform that can express the relevant construct.

docs.title: R0 — Unparseable pipeline file
docs.text: A file that could not be parsed becomes a LOW finding rather than a crash — a malformed workflow may silently not run and hides from analysis.

docs.title: R1 — Dangerous triggers
docs.text:
Privileged workflows processing attacker-controllable input.

kind detects pwn-request pull_request_target/workflow_run + checkout of PR-head code dangerous-trigger privileged untrusted trigger without a detected checkout artifact-poisoning artifact download in a workflow_run job credential-persistence checkout without persist-credentials: false on a PR-reachable workflow self-hosted-pr self-hosted runner reachable from PR events mr-untrusted-context GitLab MR job + credential-looking variables pr-context-credentials Jenkins credentials() + CHANGE_* context

FP note: pull_request_target is legitimate for labeling/triage that never touches PR code — reachability to a checkout is what escalates.

docs.title: R2 — Expression injection
docs.text:
Attacker-controllable context interpolated into a shell/script line.

kind platform expression-injection GitHub (${{ }} in run:) env-injection GitHub (untrusted value into $GITHUB_ENV/OUTPUT/PATH) script-injection GitHub (actions/github-script body) variable-injection GitLab (unquoted MR variable in script:) groovy-interpolation Jenkins (double-quoted sh with CHANGE_*/params.*)

FP note: interpolating trusted context (github.sha, matrix.*) is safe; the fix is routing the value through env: and quoting it.

docs.title: R3 — Action / image pinning
docs.text:
kind severity unpinned-third-party HIGH unpinned-first-party MEDIUM (hygiene) image-mutable-latest MEDIUM (hygiene) image-pinned-tag LOW (hygiene)

FP note: SHA pinning has an update-burden tradeoff — pair it with a dependency bot. --trusted-actions PREFIX reclassifies your org as first-party.

docs.title: R4 — Token permissions
docs.text:
missing-permissions, write-all, broad-write (≥3 write scopes), secrets-inherit (blanket secrets: inherit). All escalate in untrusted-reachable jobs. GitHub-only (guarded by the permissions capability).

FP note: some jobs legitimately need contents: write.

docs.title: R5 — Secret exposure
docs.text:
secret-echoed, secret-cli-arg, secret-untrusted-context, plaintext-secret (hardcoded high-entropy value — always redacted in output).

FP note: entropy detection also matches hashes/IDs — those are LOW confidence, and a non-secret-key denylist (name, platforms, URLs, refs) excludes common false positives.

docs.title: R6 — Step integrity
docs.text:
curl-pipe-shell (curl … | bash; HIGH over plaintext HTTP), unverified-download (download without a visible checksum; LOW), unsecure-commands (ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS).

FP note: these patterns are common in legitimate setup scripts — the remediation is checksum verification, not removal.

docs.title: How rules combine
docs.text: Rules are independent single-responsibility detectors. The risk model reads their co-occurrence: an R1 pwn-request becomes CRITICAL when R2 or R5 also fires on the same job (the exfiltration kill chain), and two distinct substantive findings on one job corroborate up a priority level — but only reach the merge-blocking P0 when the job is attacker-reachable. See Architecture.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Portcullis is a pipeline of five stages: discover → parse → normalize → assess → emit. The keystone is the normalized model — every platform parser converts its format into one shared structure, so detection rules are written once and apply to all platforms.

docs.title: The normalized model (parse once, rule once)
docs.text:
Without it, each rule would be reimplemented per platform — O(rules × platforms). Every parser instead emits:

Pipeline(platform, triggers[], permissions, jobs[], capabilities, fidelity)
  Job(name, permissions, steps[], images[], reachable_from_untrusted)
    Step(name, uses, run, env, with_, shell, line, ...)
  Trigger(event, untrusted_privileged, untrusted_input)

Rules operate on that. Adding a platform is one parser (all rules apply free); adding a rule is one function (works on all platforms free) — O(rules + platforms).

docs.title: Module layout (src layout)
docs.text:
src/portcullis/
  core/       models.py (normalized model) · taint.py · risk.py · engine.py
  platforms/  base.py · github_actions.py · gitlab_ci.py · jenkins.py
  rules/      triggers R1 · injection R2 · pinning R3 · permissions R4
              secrets R5 · integrity R6 · common.py
  emitters/   json · html · sarif · md
  cli.py · logging_config.py · py.typed

Dependencies point inward: core/ depends on nothing internal; parsers, rules, and emitters depend on core; the engine and CLI wire them together.

docs.title: The core insight: trigger-context escalation
docs.text:
A finding inside a job an attacker can reach (reachable_from_untrusted) is escalated one severity level. The same expression-injection is HIGH/P1 on a push trigger and CRITICAL/P0 under pull_request_target. This — not per-line linting — is what makes Portcullis a risk-ranker, and it reserves the merge-blocking P0 bucket for genuinely reachable criticals.

Priority P0–P3 is a deterministic function of severity, confidence, reachability, and corroboration; the pipeline security score is a transparent formula printed on every report:

score = max(0, 100 − 30·|P0| − 15·|P1| − 5·|P2| − 1·|P3|)

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text: Static-only (never executes pipeline content) · offline (no network at scan time) · deterministic output · warn-and-continue (one bad file never aborts a scan) · hardened against alias bombs, oversized files, symlink traversal, and report XSS. See the Threat Model.

docs.title: Portcullis vs. the landscape
docs.text: An honest positioning of Portcullis against existing research and tooling, written July 2026. Prior art is acknowledged, not hidden: several excellent tools cover parts of this space, and combining scanners is a legitimate strategy — a 2026 comparative study of nine GitHub Actions scanners (arXiv:2601.14455) explicitly found that no single scanner covers all identified weakness categories and recommended layering complementary tools.

docs.title: The research base
docs.text:
• ARGUS (USENIX Security 2023) introduced staged static taint analysis for GitHub workflows and the actions they call, evaluating 2.7M workflows and finding 4,307 injectable ones. It validates the core premise Portcullis is built on: untrusted context → shell sink is the dominant, findable pipeline vulnerability class. ARGUS goes deeper on GitHub (it analyzes action source code); Portcullis trades that depth for multi-platform breadth, determinism, and a CI-gate-shaped UX.
  • "Unpacking Security Scanners for GitHub Actions Workflows" (arXiv:2601.14455) identifies the weakness categories that matter (unpinned dependencies, excessive permissions, injection, secrets exposure, artifact integrity) — Portcullis rules R1–R6 map onto all five — and documents wild inconsistency between tools' false-positive philosophies (e.g., 125 vs. 3,620 artifact-integrity findings on the same corpus). Portcullis's answer to that problem is structural: confidence bands, hygiene-class demotion, and LOW-confidence findings capped at P3 so they surface without blocking.

docs.title: Tool-by-tool
docs.text: Portcullis zizmor poutine actionlint Checkov / KICS OpenSSF Scorecard Platforms GitHub + GitLab + Jenkins GitHub only GitHub + GitLab GitHub only many IaC types, shallow CI rules GitHub repo-level Trigger-context severity escalation yes — first-class partial (persona levels) partial no no no Taint source→sink for injection yes (curated lists, honest confidence) yes (template-injection) yes partial no no Priority model + 0–100 score yes, deterministic + documented formula severity/persona severity n/a severity 0–10 aggregate Outputs JSON, HTML (self-contained), SARIF, Markdown JSON, SARIF, GitHub annotations JSON, SARIF annotations many JSON Merge gate (--fail-on) yes yes yes exit code yes no Offline / no network always mostly (some online audits) yes yes yes needs API Inline suppressions yes (# portcullis: ignore[R2]) yes yes yes yes n/a Rule count 6 rules / ~25 checks 39 audits ~a dozen rules many (lint-focused) thousands (IaC-wide) ~20 checks

docs.title: What Portcullis does that the others don't
docs.text:
1. One normalized model across GitHub, GitLab, and Jenkins. zizmor and actionlint are GitHub-only; poutine covers GitLab but not Jenkins. Every Portcullis rule runs unchanged on all three platforms because parsers normalize first — and adding CircleCI/Azure is a parser, not a rule rewrite.
  2. Context escalation as the ranking backbone. The same curl | bash is P2 on a push trigger and escalates toward P0 inside a pull_request_target job. Other tools encode some of this per-rule; Portcullis applies it uniformly in the risk model, with a truth table in the test suite.
  3. Calibration as architecture, not tuning. Confidence is a first-class field; LOW confidence hard-caps at P3; hygiene findings can't corroborate their way into P0; Jenkins findings are structurally capped at MEDIUM because a Groovy parse cannot honestly claim more.
  4. A self-contained HTML report readable by a non-author, with the score formula printed next to the score and a limitations footer — plus a Markdown emitter sized for PR comments.

docs.title: What the others do that Portcullis doesn't (yet)
docs.text:
Stated plainly, per the no-overclaiming rule:

  • zizmor has ~39 audits including online ones Portcullis deliberately omits (known-vulnerable actions, impostor commits, stale refs), cache poisoning heuristics, and auto-fix mode.
  • ARGUS analyzes the source of called actions (JavaScript/composite), catching taint flows Portcullis's shallow uses: handling cannot see.
  • poutine detects known-vulnerable third-party components via its database; Portcullis is offline-only by design and does not.
  • actionlint is a full workflow-syntax linter (shellcheck integration, runner-label validation); Portcullis is not a linter and skips all of that.
  • Checkov/KICS bring compliance-framework mappings (CIS, PCI-DSS).

These gaps are tracked in VISION.md's roadmap where they fit Portcullis's offline-first thesis (deep reusable-workflow following, opt-in online mode for known-compromised versions).

docs.title: Checks adopted from this review (July 2026)
docs.text:
The landscape review directly produced these additions, each credited to the pattern's public documentation:

New check Prior art R1 credential-persistence (checkout persists token on PR-driven workflows) zizmor artipacked R1 artifact-poisoning (artifact download under workflow_run) documented artifact-poisoning attack class; zizmor/poutine R2 env-injection (untrusted context → $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT/$GITHUB_PATH) zizmor github-env R4 secrets-inherit (blanket secret forwarding to reusable workflows) zizmor secrets-inherit R6 unsecure-commands (ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS) zizmor insecure-commands Inline portcullis: ignore[...] suppressions standard across zizmor/poutine/actionlint Markdown PR-comment output zizmor/poutine GitHub integrations

docs.title: Real-world evaluation
docs.text:
Portcullis was run against pipeline files from 10 well-known open-source projects (not synthetic fixtures) to validate robustness, calibration, and output quality, and to compare head-to-head with zizmor where the platforms overlap. This is reproducible — the method is below.

Responsible-use note. Nothing here claims any project is exploitable. Findings on real repositories are pattern observations at a stated confidence; several are patterns the maintainers have already reviewed and intentionally accepted. No exploit was written, run, or attempted, and no network access occurred during any scan.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
Project Platform Pipeline files pallets/flask, pallets/click GitHub Actions 11 tiangolo/fastapi GitHub Actions 22 psf/requests GitHub Actions 8 actions/runner GitHub Actions 13 spring-projects/spring-petclinic GitHub Actions 3 gitlab-org/gitlab-runner, gitlab-org/cli GitLab CI 4 gitlab-com/.../common-ci-tasks GitLab CI 1 jenkinsci/pipeline-examples Jenkins 4

66 real pipeline files across all three platforms.

docs.title: Robustness & performance
docs.text:
• 66 files scanned in ~1.4s. Zero crashes. Real workflows include matrix jobs, reusable-workflow calls, anchors, multi-document YAML, and a deliberately-broken test fixture — all handled.
  • 2 genuine parse failures degraded to LOW R0 findings, never crashes: a .gitlab-ci.yml test fixture with a duplicate key, and a Jenkins global-library Groovy file with no pipeline block. Both are correct calls.
  • Redaction held: 0 secret-value leaks across JSON + HTML + SARIF + Markdown on the entire dataset.

docs.title: Calibration: the score ranking is sensible
docs.text:
Portcullis scored well-maintained projects high and problematic ones low, with actionable findings driving every low score:

Project Score Worst priority Character of findings gitlab-runner 100 — clean glab-cli, jenkins-examples 99 P3 one low-confidence note each flask, click 95 P2 first-party pinning hygiene requests, common-ci-tasks 85 P1/P2 pinning + permissions hygiene spring-petclinic 27 P1 unverified downloads + broad permissions actions/runner 0 P1 third-party pinning + broad-write on release jobs fastapi 0 P0 secrets used in workflow_run-triggered jobs

docs.title: Two calibration bugs this dataset caught (and we fixed)
docs.text:
Running on real data — not fixtures — is what surfaced these. Both fixes ship in 0.1.0 with regression tests.

  1. Over-escalation of hygiene into P0. Three docker/* actions pinned to version tags in actions/runner's manually-dispatched image-publish job were corroborating up to P0 (the merge-blocking bucket). P0 is meant for attacker-reachable criticals — hygiene on a trusted-trigger job shouldn't reach it. Fix: corroboration now floors at P1 unless the job is untrusted-reachable. Result: actions/runner P0s went 6 → 0, its worst is now a correct P1. (test_corroboration_on_trusted_job_floors_at_p1_never_p0)
  2. Plaintext-secret false positives. High-entropy but structurally non-secret values — platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64, artifact name: fields, a project-url: — were flagged (correctly LOW/P3, but noisy). Fix: a non-secret-key denylist plus rejecting path/list/URL-shaped values. Result: plaintext-secret findings across the dataset went 9 → 0 with no loss of genuine detections. (test_non_secret_keys_not_flagged_as_plaintext)

Aggregate effect: dataset-wide priority mix improved from P0:9 P1:27 P2:72 P3:30 to P0:3 P1:33 P2:72 P3:21 — the three remaining P0s are a single genuinely-interesting true-positive class (below), not noise.

docs.title: The one P0 pattern class worth surfacing
docs.text: In fastapi, three P0 findings flag repository secrets used inside jobs triggered by workflow_run (deploy-docs.yml, smokeshow.yml), all at MEDIUM confidence. workflow_run fires after another workflow completes — including workflows started by fork pull requests — so a secret-using job on that trigger is exactly the context class Portcullis is built to elevate. This is not a claim of exploitability: reachability depends on details static analysis can't fully prove (hence MEDIUM confidence), and the pattern is one the fastapi maintainers have already reviewed and suppressed for their own scanner. Portcullis's trigger-context lens simply re-surfaces it for a human to confirm — which is the intended behavior.

docs.title: Head-to-head vs zizmor 1.27.0 (same inputs, offline)
docs.text:
zizmor is the strongest GitHub-only comparison. Run config-free on identical inputs:

Project zizmor Portcullis Notes flask, click, requests clean (inline # zizmor: ignore in repo) 85–95, hygiene only strong agreement spring-petclinic 22 findings (7 high, 6 medium) 13 findings (0 P0, 2 P1) both flag it; both agree it needs work actions/runner 230 findings (66 high) 81 findings (0 P0, 10 P1) philosophy divergence (below) GitLab / Jenkins files "no audit was performed" — unsupported scanned all 8, scores 85–100 Portcullis-only capability

Three honest takeaways:

  1. Directional agreement. Independently, both tools rank the same projects healthy vs. problematic. That Portcullis flags what zizmor flags (unpinned actions, missing/loose permissions on actions/runner and spring-petclinic) is corroboration that it catches real issues, not noise.
  2. Different calibration philosophy — by design. zizmor is lint-style: its blanket policy makes every unpinned action (first-party included) an error, producing 230 findings / 66 "high" on actions/runner. Portcullis distinguishes first-party (P2 hygiene) from third-party (P1), reserves P0 for attacker-reachable criticals, and produces 81 findings / 0 P0. The 2026 scanner-comparison study (arXiv:2601.14455) documents exactly this spread across tools (e.g. 125 vs 3,620 findings on one corpus) and recommends layering complementary scanners — Portcullis is a priority-first, multi-platform layer, not a zizmor replacement.
  3. Platform breadth is a real, demonstrated gap. zizmor (and actionlint) are GitHub-only; on the GitLab and Jenkins files here zizmor exits with "no audit was performed." Portcullis scanned all of them through the same rule set. For a shop running mixed CI, that is the deciding difference.

docs.title: Reproduce it
docs.text:
mkdir pc-eval && cd pc-eval
for r in pallets/flask pallets/click tiangolo/fastapi psf/requests \
         actions/runner spring-projects/spring-petclinic; do
  git clone --depth 1 "https://github.com/$r" "$(basename "$r")"
done
git clone --depth 1 https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner
git clone --depth 1 https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli glab-cli
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/jenkinsci/pipeline-examples

# scan each; well-maintained repos score high, problematic ones low
for d in */; do portcullis scan "$d" --format md --out "reports/$d" --quiet; done

Portcullis version at evaluation: 0.1.0. zizmor version: 1.27.0. Third-party scan outputs are intentionally not committed to this repo.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: All numbers are reproducible with the commands shown. Environment: Python 3.11, a laptop-class machine; your throughput will vary but the shape holds.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
Workload Files Findings Time Throughput Bundled GitHub fixtures 2 11 ~12 ms — Real-world set (10 OSS repos) 66 ~130 ~1.4 s ~47 files/s* Synthetic vulnerable workflows 500 2,500 ~1.4 s ~360 files/s

* The real-world set includes git-clone and disk I/O across three platforms; the synthetic set isolates parse+rules throughput.

Portcullis is single-pass and CPU-light; scanning a typical repository's handful of pipeline files is effectively instant, and even a monorepo with hundreds of workflows scans in seconds.

Reproduce the synthetic benchmark:

import time, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from portcullis.core.engine import scan
from portcullis.core.models import ScanConfig

wf = ("on: pull_request_target\npermissions: write-all\njobs:\n  j:\n"
      "    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - run: echo hi\n")
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    wd = Path(d) / ".github" / "workflows"; wd.mkdir(parents=True)
    for i in range(500):
        (wd / f"wf{i}.yml").write_text(wf)
    t = time.time(); r = scan(Path(d), ScanConfig())
    print(len(r.files_scanned), "files in", round(time.time() - t, 2), "s")

docs.title: Robustness
docs.text:
On the real-world set of 66 files from 10 well-known projects (Flask, FastAPI, requests, actions/runner, gitlab-runner, jenkinsci/pipeline-examples, …):

  • Zero crashes. Matrix jobs, reusable workflows, YAML anchors, multi-document YAML, and even a deliberately-broken file were all handled.
  • Two genuinely-malformed files degraded to LOW R0 findings (warn-and-continue).
  • Zero secret-value leaks across all four output formats.

docs.title: Memory & footprint
docs.text:
• One runtime dependency (ruamel.yaml) — the whole install is small.
  • Memory scales with the size of one file at a time, not the whole tree; the parser refuses files over 2 MB and caps YAML expansion at 2M nodes (billion-laughs hardening), so a hostile file cannot exhaust memory.

docs.title: Accuracy / calibration
docs.text: Portcullis is calibrated for low false-positive noise, not maximal findings. On the real-world set it agreed directionally with a mature competitor (zizmor) on which repos were healthy vs. problematic, while producing a prioritized, lower-volume result (e.g. 81 findings / 0 P0 where a blanket linter reported 230 / 66 "high" on the same repo). Two calibration bugs found on real data were fixed with regression tests. Full detail: Real-world Evaluation.

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
Platform Files Fidelity GitHub Actions .github/workflows/*.y*ml full GitLab CI .gitlab-ci.yml full Jenkins Jenkinsfile best-effort (Groovy; findings capped at MEDIUM confidence)

Outputs: JSON, self-contained HTML (CSP-hardened), SARIF 2.1.0 (schema-validated), Markdown.

docs.title: Portcullis ↔ OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks
docs.text:
Portcullis's detection rules map directly onto the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks (Krivelevich & Gil, 2022) — the industry-standard taxonomy for pipeline security. This is Portcullis's natural framework fit: it is a CI/CD security tool, so it speaks the CI/CD Top-10 language rather than, say, the LLM/GenAI lists that target a different problem domain.

Each Portcullis finding kind is listed under the OWASP risk it evidences. A single rule can touch more than one risk.

OWASP CI/CD risk What it means Portcullis rules / kinds CICD-SEC-1 — Insufficient Flow Control changes reach sensitive stages without adequate review/gating (partial) Portcullis is a gate mechanism for this risk via --fail-on; it detects the config that makes flow control matter, and its own CI is the reference gate CICD-SEC-2 — Inadequate Identity & Access Mgmt over-permissioned identities/tokens R4 missing-permissions, write-all, broad-write CICD-SEC-3 — Dependency Chain Abuse pulling in code you don't control / can't verify R3 unpinned-third-party, unpinned-first-party; R6 curl-pipe-shell, unverified-download CICD-SEC-4 — Poisoned Pipeline Execution (PPE) attacker-controlled code runs in the pipeline R1 pwn-request, dangerous-trigger, self-hosted-pr; R2 all injection kinds (expression-injection, env-injection, script-injection, variable-injection, groovy-interpolation) CICD-SEC-5 — Insufficient Pipeline-Based Access Controls a compromised step can do more than it should R4 (scope of the job token); the trigger-context escalation model is a direct expression of PBAC thinking CICD-SEC-6 — Insufficient Credential Hygiene secrets exposed, over-shared, or long-lived R5 secret-echoed, secret-cli-arg, secret-untrusted-context, plaintext-secret; R4 secrets-inherit; R1 credential-persistence CICD-SEC-7 — Insecure System Configuration dangerous platform settings enabled R6 unsecure-commands (ACTIONS_ALLOW_UNSECURE_COMMANDS) CICD-SEC-8 — Ungoverned Usage of 3rd-Party Services unvetted external actions/services R3 third-party pinning (the --trusted-actions allowlist is the governance knob) CICD-SEC-9 — Improper Artifact Integrity Validation trusting artifacts/downloads that could be tampered R1 artifact-poisoning; R6 curl-pipe-shell, unverified-download; R3 image digest pinning CICD-SEC-10 — Insufficient Logging & Visibility can't see what the pipeline did (out of scope for a static scanner — Portcullis analyzes config, not runtime logs; noted honestly)

docs.title: Coverage summary
docs.text: Portcullis provides detection coverage for 8 of the 10 OWASP CI/CD risks (SEC-2 through SEC-9), acts as an enforcement mechanism for SEC-1 (flow control via the merge gate), and honestly does not cover SEC-10 (runtime logging/visibility), which is a runtime-observability concern outside a static scanner's remit.

docs.title: Why this mapping matters
docs.text:
• For adopters: it lets a security team place Portcullis in a framework they already use for CI/CD risk, and shows exactly which risks it does and does not address — no overclaiming.
  • For contribution: the OWASP CI/CD project welcomes methodology and analysis contributions; this mapping (plus Portcullis's real-world evaluation and the trigger-context reachability model) is the kind of practical, tool-backed material that fits an OWASP methodology or research contribution.

Honesty note. This maps Portcullis onto a published OWASP taxonomy; it does not claim endorsement by or affiliation with OWASP. The CICD-SEC identifiers and definitions are OWASP's; the rule mapping is ours.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text: Portcullis is a pipeline-security gate: a static analyzer that catches the CI/CD misconfigurations behind real pipeline compromises — untrusted code executing in privileged contexts, expression injection, mutable supply-chain references, over-broad tokens, exposed secrets — and prioritizes them by whether attacker-controlled input can actually reach them.

docs.title: Who it's for
docs.text:
• Platform / security engineers gating merges on pipeline hygiene across many repositories.
  • Teams hardening CI after an incident or audit, who need traceable findings with concrete remediations, not a wall of lint.

docs.title: What makes it worth building
docs.text: Trigger-context reasoning. A YAML linter flags a curl | bash everywhere it appears; Portcullis knows the one inside a pull_request_target job that checks out PR code is a different class of problem, and escalates it. Risk is contextual, not per-line — that judgment is encoded in the risk model, the priority function, and the score.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Not a general YAML linter. Style, schema completeness, and syntax nits belong elsewhere.
  • Not SAST for application code. Portcullis reads pipeline definitions, not the code the pipeline builds.
  • Not a whole-repo secrets scanner. R5 covers secrets in pipeline files and pipeline context only; dedicated secret scanners cover the rest of the tree.
  • Not a runtime monitor. Static, pre-merge analysis only.

docs.title: Roadmap (demand-driven)
docs.text:
1. Deep reusable-workflow following (the biggest fidelity gain).
  2. Opt-in online mode: resolve action tags to SHAs, flag known-compromised versions — default stays offline.
  3. More platforms behind the same normalized model: CircleCI, Azure Pipelines, Buildkite.
  4. Auto-fix suggestions as diffs (route through env:, pin to SHA).
  5. Richer suppression: inline portcullis: ignore[...] comments shipped in 0.1.0; next is a reviewed suppression file (VEX-style, with owner and expiry) for org-level acceptance workflows.

docs.title: Threat model — for Portcullis itself
docs.text: A security tool is attack surface. This document states what Portcullis does with the untrusted input it consumes and what it guarantees about its own behavior.

docs.title: What Portcullis consumes
docs.text: Pipeline definition files (.github/workflows/*.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile) from arbitrary repositories. These are untrusted input: a scanned repository may be attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
1. Never executes pipeline content. Files are parsed (ruamel.yaml for YAML; a regex/structural scanner for Groovy). No eval, no subprocess of scanned content, no Groovy runtime. The Jenkins parser deliberately trades fidelity for safety — Groovy cannot be evaluated safely, so it never is.
  2. No network access at scan time. No resolving action tags against a registry, no fetching called workflows, no telemetry. pip install is the only network-touching operation, and it happens before any scan.
  3. Malformed input degrades, never escalates. Any parse failure — malformed YAML, non-UTF-8 bytes, empty files, absurd nesting — becomes a warning plus a LOW R0 finding. One bad file never aborts a scan (tested in tests/test_edge_cases.py).
  4. Detected secrets are redacted. When R5 flags a plaintext credential-shaped value, the value never appears in any output format — evidence strings carry only length and entropy metadata. Redaction is explicitly tested against all three emitters.
  5. Deterministic output. Same input tree → byte-identical JSON/HTML/SARIF/Markdown (the single top-level timestamp excepted), so reports are diffable and a tampered rerun is detectable.
  6. Suppressions are never silent. Inline portcullis: ignore comments drop a finding from the findings list but are themselves reported (file, line, rule) in every output format — an attacker quietly suppressing a finding leaves a visible trace.

docs.title: Denial-of-service hardening (parser)
docs.text:
Because pipeline files come from untrusted repositories, the parser is hardened against a malicious file trying to hang or exhaust a scan — important when Portcullis runs as a CI gate on pull-request content:

  • YAML alias bombs ("billion laughs"). ruamel's round-trip loader keeps aliases as shared references, so a bomb parses instantly but explodes when traversed (e.g. str() on an env value). After loading, any alias-bearing document is walked with a hard node budget (MAX_YAML_NODES, 2,000,000) that short-circuits, so a bomb is refused in bounded time (~0.6 s) regardless of its nominal expansion (10⁸–10¹³ nodes), while legitimate anchor reuse — dozens of jobs sharing a <<: *default merge — is unaffected. Regression: tests/test_security.py.
  • Oversized files. Files larger than MAX_FILE_BYTES (2 MB — orders of magnitude above any real pipeline file) are skipped with a LOW finding rather than read into memory, bounding parse time, regex work, and memory.
  • Deep nesting. ruamel raises on excessive recursion; the engine catches it and degrades the file to a LOW finding instead of crashing.
  • Regex safety. Detection patterns avoid nested quantifiers; worst-case behavior is linear-to-quadratic in a single line's length, which the file size cap bounds — no catastrophic (exponential) backtracking.

docs.title: Confidentiality & integrity of the scan
docs.text:
• Symlinks are not followed. A pipeline file that is a symlink is skipped, not read — a malicious repo cannot use .gitlab-ci.yml → /etc/passwd to make Portcullis read an arbitrary host file into its report. os.walk does not descend into symlinked directories either. Regression: tests/test_security.py.
  • Report is derived from hostile input, but inert. Evidence strings originate in scanned files. The HTML emitter escapes all interpolated content (html.escape(quote=True)), and — as defense-in-depth — the report carries a strict Content-Security-Policy (default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline') so no script can execute and no network request can be made even if an escaping bug ever slipped through. The report is fully self-contained, so the CSP never affects rendering. Regression: tests/test_security.py.

docs.title: Residual risks
docs.text:
• YAML parser attack surface. ruamel.yaml still processes hostile input; it is the project's one runtime dependency, version-bounded in pyproject.toml, and chosen over unsafe loaders (no !!python/object construction — the round-trip loader rejects arbitrary tags, so YAML cannot execute code). The node-budget and size caps above bound its resource use.
  • Findings are advice. Portcullis output gates merges; a wrong LOW/clean verdict is possible (see Limitations in README). It is one layer, not an authorization system.
  • Markdown output is for trusted renderers. The Markdown emitter escapes table-breaking characters; it is intended for GitHub/GitLab PR comments, which sanitize HTML. Do not render Portcullis Markdown through a non- sanitizing HTML renderer on untrusted input — use the HTML report (CSP- protected) for that.

docs.title: Fixture policy
docs.text: The repository's own test fixtures are deliberately vulnerable but inert: echo-only payloads, example.com URLs, fake-marked secret-shaped strings. An automated guard (tests/test_inertness.py) fails the build if a fixture ever contains a functional exploit shape, a real-looking credential, or a non-inert URL.
